notes.title: Chapter map: System prompts & agent instructions
notes.html:
The authored text around every request, once it outgrows one person. Note 55 is the operating model (owned layers, one rule per case). Note 56 is why a layer outranks another, and that it's a trained preference. Notes 57 and 58 are two surfaces worth writing well (behaviour, tools). Note 61 is how the text gets rendered. Notes 59, 60 and 62 are pointers: instructions on demand, a model writing them, and instructions passed to another agent. Read each arrow as a sentence: system prompt design is ranked by the instruction hierarchy.

Green = CORE, blue = SUPPORTING, yellow = BREADTH. The neighbouring sections are named in the last bullet.

Reading order:55 system prompt design56 instruction hierarchy57 behavioural specs58 tool descriptions61 prompt templating59 skill files60 meta-prompting62 multi-agent briefs

Owners

Idea Owner note

Authority tiers; trained, not enforced; later wins at one tier; delegation; no authority by default 56 instruction hierarchy

How tool text is worded; confusion pairs; the cross-reference; negative space 58 tool descriptions
Resident against on-demand instructions; skill and instruction files as prompt text 59 skill files
A model writing a prompt, without a score 60 meta-prompting
A value is data, a template is code; 2^N renderings; fragments above the cache line, conditionals below 61 prompt templating
The brief as prompt text 62 multi-agent briefs
The six regions prompt anatomy, not these notes
The three message roles; no outside variable in system system, user and prefill, not these notes
Behaviour, threshold and fallback in one clause; emphasis instruction writing, not these notes
A role sets voice, not accuracy the role line, not note 57
Strip and wrap a delimiter delimiters, not note 61
Prefix stability, canonical bytes, the two-process check context ordering, not notes 55 and 61
Cohorts of a golden set golden datasets, not note 57
Gating a change in CI regression suites, not note 55
Versions, rollout, tenant overrides versioning, decoupled release, multi-tenant prompts, not note 55
Scored prompt search APE, not note 60
A role is not a permission; extraction prompt injection, prompt extraction, not note 56
What a definition contains; the call round trip tool schemas, function calling (Agentic), not note 58
Which tools to have; too many tools tool design, selection at scale (Agentic), not note 58
MCP mechanics; pinning third-party definitions MCP, MCP at scale (Agentic), not note 58
Orchestration; what crosses a hand-off orchestrator-worker, delegation (Agentic), not note 62
Hooks, permission modes, how a harness loads skills harness mechanics (Agentic), not note 59

Older text of every note is in 08-Prompt-engineering/_superseded/06-System Prompts & Agent Instructions/. No tier changed and nothing merged. The cache arithmetic and canonical serialisation left 55 and 61 for note 48; the fleet capacity table and the promotion pipeline left 55 for sections 09 and 12; the 30-tools answer in 58 now defers to the Agentic note.

Where does this instruction live?

The first question is the simpler rung: most new rules should be an edit to an old one, or nothing.

Anything that varies per request is not an instruction at all: it goes in the user turn as data.

  • Edit (55): if the old clause exists for a different case and has its own test, a separate rule with a written precedence is cleaner.
  • Code (56): if failure costs little, a request and an output count may be enough.
  • Tool description (58): if the rule compares several tools, it's cross-tool policy, so it goes in system.
  • 📜 System prompt (57): if a tenant may change it, it becomes a named setting, not free text.
  • 📂 Skill (59): if your platform has no way to load files on demand, retrieve the text in your assembly code, or keep it resident.

A second choice, drawn in its owner note: conditionals or fragments? (61). Would one flat prompt do? Yes for a few endpoints. Otherwise fixed fragments above the cache line, conditionals below it.

At a glance

Note What it adds Extra cost per request Fails as What enforces it

Instruction hierarchy named delegation a line of text; a settings surface preference overwhelmed renderer, permissions
Behavioural specs five clauses resident tokens improvised fallback; over-refusal nothing per clause: a request
Tool descriptions when not, cross-reference, negative space description tokens confusion pair; invented fields schema for shape only
Skill files text loaded on demand metadata always; body on a match never triggers; untrusted skill nothing: context only
Meta-prompting a drafted prompt none at run time reads better, scores worse your eval
Prompt templating strict rendering, fragments none code run from template text; untested branches the renderer, CI
Multi-agent briefs four-part brief brief tokens per worker overlap, vague scope return validated in code

Lineage

2023 System role in chat APIs a home for authored text 🟢 Established
Apr 2024 The instruction hierarchy all text weighted alike 🟡 Maturing

Landscape (as of Oct 2026)

Every row was read from the linked page on 31 Oct 2026.

Who outranks whom

OpenAI Anthropic

Source Model Spec 2026-10-29, text guide Claude's constitution

Tool text

Anthropic OpenAI Google (Gemini API)

When to use it in the description, including when not to "use the system prompt to describe when (and when not)" "provide context and instructions"

Source define tools, prompting guide function calling function calling

Instruction and skill files

Format Facts Source
AGENTS.md plain Markdown, no required fields; closest file wins; explicit chat prompts override it; stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation agents.md
CLAUDE.md context, not enforced configuration; target under 200 lines; every file found is concatenated, root first; AGENTS.md read by default only when no CLAUDE.md exists Claude Code: memory
SKILL.md required name (64 characters) and description (1,024); metadata about 100 tokens, body under 5k, under 500 lines; references one level deep Agent Skills spec, Anthropic overview

Guidance on prompts themselves

Topic Vendor statement Source

Prompt generators Playground Generate uses meta-prompts; the Console has a generator and an improver OpenAI, Anthropic

Four bullets

  • The one big idea: instructions need owners. Every note here answers one question about a sentence: who wrote it, who may change it, where it lives, what ranks it, and what proves it still earns its place.
  • The two most-confused pairs: rank vs permission (56: what the model prefers against what your code allows) · template injection vs prompt injection (61: on your server before the model, against read by the model).
  • Ten minutes before an interview: note 55's window table and Break it, note 56's trust diagram, note 57's anatomy block, note 58's region ③, and the tree above.
  • Cross-section links: the attacks on this text are prompt injection and prompt extraction; shipping it is prompt versioning; the runtime it sits in is the prompt-layer reference architecture. Content gaps: no note on detecting contradictions between differently named rules (55's Break it catches only id collisions); no note on writing instructions for a long-running coding repository beyond the pointer in 59.

notes.title: System Prompt Design at Scale — A Composed, Owned, Tested Artifact, Not a String
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: prompting best practices · Anthropic Engineering: effective context engineering · Anthropic: published system prompts · OpenAI Model Spec, 2026-10-29

TL;DR

Writing one system prompt is easy. Keeping it true is the job: it gains a rule per incident, nobody owns the rules, and two of them end up in a conflict the model settles silently. So treat it as a build product: layers with owners, composed by code, every rule tied to a test that fails without it. The text stays a request. What is enforced is the composition, the gate and the rollback.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchdesign time
Flow:platform layerteam layersession layer ─composer joins in fixed orderconflict checkone eval case per ruleversioned releasechange a rule and its case, or delete both

Recall

Prompt Answer
Where does a sentence go? True on every request: system. Varies: user turn. One tool: its description.
How does a system prompt rot? One rule per incident, none removed, conflicts settled silently.
What makes a rule safe to delete? A case that fails without it, and its recorded reason.
Why isn't a diff review enough? The prompt is one conditioning prefix, so effects aren't local to the edit.
What still holds if the model ignores the prompt? Layer order, the eval gate, rollback, and controls in code.
Draw by hand: the layers Tools, platform, team, session, cache line, request: each with owner and change rate.

The idea

A support prompt says "Don't discuss refunds over $500" and, forty lines later, "Always resolve the customer's issue in one message". A customer asks for an $800 refund. Both rules apply and they disagree. The model picks one, on this run, and no log says which rule lost. Six people wrote this prompt over a year, each line answers a real incident, and nobody dares delete anything.

No sentence is bad. The prompt has no owners, no record of why a rule exists, and no test that a rule still earns its place.

So change what the prompt is. It stops being one string and becomes layers with different owners, joined by a composer no team can bypass. Each rule carries an id, the incident behind it and a case that fails without it. A conflict becomes a decision someone writes down: here, the refund limit becomes a route with a named action, so "resolve in one message" has nothing left to fight.

Every sentence is still a request. What you added is enforced around it.

The trade: you pay for a composer, a rule-to-case map and a release path; you buy a prompt that can be changed, audited and pruned. With one team and one prompt, a file and a test suite are enough.

How it works

The prompt after the split, one region per owner. The six regions themselves belong to prompt anatomy.

① CONSTRAINTS  Never show an account the caller isn't verified for.      ← platform: teams can't edit it
② ROLE         You are Acme's billing assistant.                         ← team: one line
③ TASK         Answer billing questions from tool results only.          ← team: the one job
④ CONSTRAINTS  Refund over $500 or legal question: escalate_to_human.    ← team: a rule with a case
⑤ OUTPUT       At most three sentences. Quote the field you used.        ← team: code can check it
⑥ CONTEXT      <tenant>{{settings}}</tenant> <ticket>{{ticket}}</ticket> ← user turn: data

Those regions land in this order in the window.

Region Owner Changes every Cached
Tool definitions owning team release yes
Platform layer: safety, data handling, escalation platform team policy change yes, shared by every agent
Team layer: role, task, scope, output owning team release yes, per agent
Session layer: tenant choices, rendered by you your config session yes, per tenant
— last cache breakpoint —
Date, retrieved text, the ticket whoever sent it request no

Why the order pays is owned by context ordering; why a value mustn't enter the upper rows is owned by system, user and prefill.

Rule What actually happens
Teams emit fragments No team writes a whole prompt. The composer joins layers in a fixed order, so nobody can move or drop the platform layer.
One rule, one case A rule links to the case that fails without it and the incident behind it. Without those, "can we delete this?" has no answer.
Conflicts get decided Two rules at one tier need a written precedence: authority tiers say nothing about them.
Rules leave when they can Output shape goes to a schema, one tool's guidance to its description, a rare procedure to a skill, a must-hold rule to code.

Which surface takes a sentence is the chapter map's tree.

Evolution

Lineage:2023 chat APIs add a system roleApr–May 2024 instruction hierarchy, Model Spec draft2024 Anthropic starts publishing its app system promptsSep 2025 "minimal doesn't mean short"Oct 2025 skills move rare procedures out of the resident prompt
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026): structured system prompts are in every provider's guide, and Anthropic publishes its own. Composing fragments across teams is less settled.
  • Stronger-model test: partly. Anthropic's guide says recent models follow instructions closely, so heavy emphasis and defensive rules can go. What won't change: a model can't settle your product's conflict, or know who owns a rule or why it exists.
  • Checked on: Anthropic's guide, read 31 Oct 2026, for its current models.

Code

The accreted prompt against the layered one, on one request.

🔴 Naive 🟢 Engineered
Prompt (the part that differs) Today is {{date}}. Don't discuss refunds over $500. Always resolve the issue in one message. regions ①–⑥ above; the date moves to the user turn
On the input "charged twice, refund $800 to my card" two rules apply; one is dropped looks up the account, then escalates with the amount
Fails as silent conflict; an invented account fact; a changing first line, so no cache hit —
The one edit — ④ turning a prohibition into a route: the rule now names what to do, so a case can check it

Break it: the belief that layers which pass their own checks compose into a safe prompt.

platform = {"refund_limit": "Refunds over $500: call escalate_to_human."}
team = {"refund_limit": "Resolve every refund in this chat.", "tone": "Warm, short."}
tests = {"refund_limit": "case-118", "tone": "case-204"}     # rule id → the case that fails without it
def compose(*layers):
    rules = {}
    for r, text in (kv for layer in layers for kv in layer.items()):
        if r in rules: raise ValueError(f"{r}: {rules[r]!r} vs {text!r}")
        rules[r] = text
    return rules
print([r for layer in (platform, team) for r in layer if r not in tests]); compose(platform, team)
# look for: an empty list (every rule has a case), then a ValueError on refund_limit
# naive belief predicts: no error, because each layer passes on its own

Run on Python 3.15, it prints [], then raises ValueError: refund_limit: 'Refunds over $500: call escalate_to_human.' vs 'Resolve every refund in this chat.'. Only ids make the collision visible: two differently named rules that contradict pass, so the safety suite also runs on the composed prompt.

Measure it

  • Offline: pass rate per cohort on the composed prompt against the live version; then delete one rule at a time and keep each deletion that changes nothing.
  • In production: refusal, escalation and tool-call rates per prompt version; rules with no case; distinct composed prefixes; cache-read tokens per request.
  • Enforced by: the composer for layer order, the CI gate for changes, and rollback. Every sentence inside the prompt is a request only.

Interview

30-second answer: Writing a system prompt is the easy part; operating one is the job. It holds what's true on every request, and it rots: a rule per incident, none removed, conflicts settled silently. So I split it into owned layers joined by a composer, tie each rule to a case that fails without it, and ship changes through an eval gate with rollback. The text stays a request.

Q · Mechanism — Why can't you review a prompt edit like a code diff? Code has locality: a change reaches what calls it. A system prompt is one conditioning prefix on every output, so tightening a refusal clause can make unrelated answers more cautious, and a format rule can suppress a behaviour you relied on. A new rule can also collide with an old one, and that shows as unpredictable answers, not a consistent bug. So review needs a broad suite that includes cases the edit has nothing to do with.

Q · Trade-off — The prompt is 4,000 tokens and growing. Do you cut it? Not by length. The simpler rung is deleting what no case needs, so I audit: give each rule a case, delete rules whose removal changes nothing, and reconcile conflicts with a written precedence. Then I move text out: format to a schema, tool guidance to descriptions, rare procedures to skills. A stable prefix is cheap once cached. I'd reach for layers and a composer only when more than one team edits it.

Q · Failure — After a prompt change, refusals jump on one tenant only. Likely a cross-layer conflict: a team or tenant fragment colliding with the platform layer, each passing its own tests. I'd confirm by comparing refusal rate per version and tenant, then diffing the composed prompt, not the fragment. Roll back first, because that's one action. The fix is a written precedence, a regression case from the incident, and running the safety suite on compositions.

Q · Design — Forty teams ship agents on shared infrastructure. The binding constraint: forty teams editing behaviour will contradict each other and your safety rules. So teams publish versioned fragments, and only the composer emits a prompt. The platform layer sits first, immutable and shared. Every fragment version must pass its own cases plus the platform suite on the composed prompt. I'd watch cross-layer failures first, then distinct prefixes, because fragments split the cache. The surrounding pieces are in the prompt-layer reference architecture and prompt versioning.

Pitfalls

  • "Shorter system prompts are better"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: every token is paid on every request, and short feels disciplined.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: Anthropic Engineering says minimal doesn't necessarily mean short, and its own app prompts are long. Length isn't free either: Claude Code's docs say longer CLAUDE.md files reduce adherence.
    ↳ Think instead: cut what no test needs, then look at the length.
  • "Adding a rule after an incident is the cheap, safe fix"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it takes a minute, and the incident stops.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it was cheap each time and expensive in total. Rules added under pressure, untested and never removed, end up contradicting each other, and boundary cases turn unpredictable.
    ↳ Think instead: a rule ships with the case that fails without it, which also makes deleting it possible.
  • "The policy is in the system prompt, so it's enforced"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "We never give financial advice" reads like a control, and it passes review.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it is a sentence the model usually follows. Reorder the file or change the model, and it can stop holding with no error anywhere.
    ↳ Think instead: the prompt states intent; a case proves it today; a control in code holds it.
  • Not the same: system prompt design vs the instruction hierarchy
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are about layers of instructions, and both get drawn as a stack.
    ↳ Difference: the hierarchy is how a model ranks sources of text. Your layers are how an organisation owns text, and all of them usually land in one tier.
    ↳ Think instead: layer order settles ownership and caching; conflicts inside a tier need a written rule.
  • Don't build a registry for one team.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the forty-team design is the impressive answer, and prompts feel unmanaged.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a composer, a registry and canaries take effort to run, and they slow the small edits a young product needs.
    ↳ Do instead: start with one file in the repo and one eval suite. Add layers when a second team edits behaviour.
  • Shelf life: how much emphasis and how many defensive rules a prompt needs will keep shrinking. Owned layers, one rule per case and non-local effects won't.

Connections

Path:system, user and prefillsystem prompt designinstruction hierarchybehavioural specsprompt templating
  • Builds on prompt anatomy: the regions each layer fills.
  • Measured by golden datasets: where the one-case-per-incident cohort lives.
  • Owned elsewhere: multi-tenant prompts owns overrides; decoupled release owns rollout.
  • Costed in provider prompt caching: the stable prefix priced.
  • Attacked by prompt extraction: assume the text is public.
  • Drilled in a system prompt of patches.

notes.title: Layered Instruction Hierarchy — Who Outranks Whom, Trained In and Never Enforced
notes.html:
References

Wallace et al. 2024: The Instruction Hierarchy · OpenAI Model Spec, 2026-10-29 · Claude's constitution · OpenAI: text generation

TL;DR

Models are trained to rank instructions by where they came from: provider above developer, developer above user, and tool output or quoted text at no authority by default. It is a trained preference, not an access check, so it degrades under pressure instead of failing closed. Use it as a design rule, say out loud what you delegate, and hold anything that must not move with a control outside the model.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchdesign time
Flow:provider rulesyour developer promptuser turntool results and quoted text as datahigher tier wins; at one tier, the later messagea control outside the model

Recall

Prompt Answer
The Model Spec's order? Root, system, developer, user, guideline; no authority by default for tool and assistant messages, quoted text.
Same tier, conflicting messages? The later message supersedes the earlier one.
What still holds if the preference fails? Only controls outside the model: permissions, output checks, approvals.

The idea

A tenant asks for their custom instructions to override your platform rules. You paste their text into the system prompt, and one line reads "refunds of any size are fine". Now the rule that protects you and the rule that weakens it sit in one tier, with nothing to say which wins.

The hierarchy can't help, because you put both on the same rung. Split your rules instead. Non-delegable rules (safety, data handling, legal duties) are yours and stay above the tenant. Delegable defaults (tone, length, scope within limits) are opinions a tenant may change. Then write the delegation down: the platform text names what the tenant may set, and your code renders only those settings.

Rank is still a request: the model usually honours it. The enforced part is what your code lets into each tier, and the check on the action.

The trade: separating and naming delegable rules takes a design pass and a settings surface; you get customers who can customise without being able to weaken what you're liable for.

How it works

Text from the red zone can always be phrased as an instruction, and only a trained preference stops it being followed.

The last box is the point: recovery is a control in code, not better wording.

Rule What actually happens
Higher tier wins A lower instruction that conflicts with a higher one is set aside. In the Model Spec (Oct 2026) root rules can't be overridden by any conversation.
Later wins, at one tier A later message at the same level supersedes an earlier one, so a user's turn thirty can replace their turn two.
Authority can be delegated "No authority" is a default: an applicable instruction can delegate. The Model Spec says a coding request implicitly delegates to AGENTS files, while tool outputs may still be malicious.
One prompt is one tier Two conflicting rules in your own prompt are peers. The hierarchy is silent, so you write the precedence.

The same tenant request, placed two ways:

🔴 Naive 🟢 Engineered
Prompt (the part that differs) tenant's free text pasted after your rules, in system Tenants may set tone and length only. plus tone={{tone}} from a closed list
On the input tenant text "refunds of any size are fine" peer of your refund rule the field doesn't exist, so it never renders
Fails as a delegable slot grants non-delegable authority —
The one edit — delegation as named settings in place of free text

Evolution

Lineage:Apr 2024 instruction hierarchy trained on GPT-3.5May 2024 Model Spec draft names a chain of commandJan 2026 Claude's constitution: principals, and conversational inputs as information29 Oct 2026 current Model Spec: six levels, delegation to tool output spelled out
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): every major provider ranks instructions, while names and semantics differ, and the ranking moves with training.
  • Stronger-model test: a stronger model holds the ranking better; it doesn't turn it into a control. What won't change: instructions and data share one channel, so rank stays a preference.
  • Checked on: the paper's method was shown on GPT-3.5 (2024). Provider documents state intended behaviour, not a measured rate.

Measure it

  • Offline: on planted conflicts per tier (tenant against platform, tool result against developer), the override rate against the same rule with no delegation text, per model version.
  • In production: blocked actions at the permission layer; a rising count means the preference is being overwhelmed and the control is carrying the load.
  • Enforced by: your renderer, for what reaches each tier, and permissions and output checks, for what must hold. The ranking itself is a request only.

Interview

30-second answer: Models are trained to weight instructions by source. OpenAI's Model Spec runs root, system, developer, user, guideline, with tool output and quoted text at no authority by default. It's a trained preference, not an access check: the tokens arrive in one stream, so it degrades under pressure. I use it to decide what goes where, and put real controls underneath.

Q · Mechanism — Why does a model obey this if nothing enforces it? Training. Wallace's method builds examples where a lower-privilege instruction tries to override a higher one, and teaches the model to follow aligned instructions and ignore misaligned ones. The result correlates compliance with role. Nothing at inference time checks it, because roles are markers in one stream. That explains both why it usually works and why a persuasive message or a long conversation can get past it.

Q · Trade-off — A tenant wants to override your platform rules. Yes or no? Split the question. The simpler rung is a flat no, which fails customers who only want a different tone. Rules you carry liability for stay non-delegable; style and scope defaults become named settings the platform layer explicitly delegates. I don't rely on ordering for the non-delegable part: a tool-level permission or output check holds it. The extra cost is a settings surface and one more test per delegated field. Overrides in full are in multi-tenant prompts.

Pitfalls

  • "The system prompt is enforced; the model can't violate it"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it is a separate API field and it usually wins.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: no check runs at inference. The ranking was trained on conflict data, which is why jailbreaks and indirect injection work at all.
    ↳ Think instead: a strong default, never a boundary.
  • "Our own corpus is trusted, so instruction-shaped text in it is no risk"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: you own the store and control access to it.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: our corpus held customer tickets, so any customer could write text that was later retrieved into a prompt. Owning the store says nothing about who wrote what's inside.
    ↳ Think instead: a trusted source is not trusted content.
  • Not the same: rank vs permission
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are described as "what this role may do".
    ↳ Difference: rank is what the model prefers among texts. A permission is what your code allows, whoever asked. Prompt injection targets the first, and the second doesn't care.
    ↳ Think instead: see a role is not a permission.
  • Don't assume tiers port across providers.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: every API has a "system" field, so the semantics look shared.
    ↳ What goes wrong: in the Model Spec system means OpenAI's messages and your text is developer. Claude's constitution says its ordering of principals is not strict. A design tuned to one ordering can shift on migration.
    ↳ Do instead: re-run the planted-conflict suite on any model or vendor change.
  • Shelf life: the tier names and delegation details are volatile (see the chapter map's Landscape). A preference that isn't a control is durable.

Connections

Path:system, user and prefillinstruction hierarchybehavioural specsindirect prompt injection
  • Builds on system, user and prefill: the roles the tiers are defined over.
  • Attacked by prompt injection: text aimed at the trained preference.
  • Enforced by defence in depth: the deterministic layers under it.
  • Used by skill and instruction files: repository files that gain delegated authority.
  • Drilled in a system prompt of patches.

notes.title: Behavioural Specs — Tone, Refusal, Escalation and the When-Unsure Clause
notes.html:
References

OpenAI Model Spec, 2026-10-29 · Anthropic: increase output consistency · Anthropic: published system prompts

TL;DR

A behavioural spec is the part of a system prompt that governs how the assistant acts, not what it knows: voice, scope, refusal, escalation, and what to do when unsure. Two moves carry it: every prohibition gets a destination, and the when-unsure clause exists. Without it, the model invents a fallback per phrasing. Each clause is a classifier with two errors, so test what it should catch and what it shouldn't.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchdesign time
Flow:voicescope, naming the outsiderefusal with a destinationescalation trigger and actionwhen unsurea case per clause, both directionsover-refusal gated like under-refusal

Recall

Prompt Answer
The clause teams omit? When-unsure: without it the fallback is improvised, differently each time.
What makes a refusal testable? A named action: escalate, ask, or offer X. One right output exists.
What does a refusal rule still need? A near-miss cohort, or over-refusal goes unseen.

The idea

The prompt says "Never make anything up." A customer asks for their renewal date and the tool result doesn't include it. The bot can't state a date and has no instruction for that case, so it hedges every sentence. On a differently phrased question it guesses, and on a third it asks something back.

Nobody wrote a bad rule. The prompt drew a line and left no path, so the model filled the gap, and it filled it differently each time. Add one clause: "If a tool result lacks what you need, say what you couldn't determine, then call escalate_to_human." Now the widest and least tested part of the behaviour has one right output, and you can write a case for it.

Each clause is still a request, and most interactions have nothing else governing them: filters and permissions cover only the actions you thought to wrap.

The trade: a spec adds resident tokens and tests to maintain; it buys consistent behaviour at the edges, where hedging and invented fallbacks live. An extraction endpoint needs none of it.

How it works

Five clauses, in the order the model reads them. Each is one well-formed instruction.

① ROLE         You are Acme's billing assistant. Direct, warm, no filler.          ← voice, one line
② CONSTRAINTS  Scope: billing, invoices, plans. Not legal, tax, other accounts.    ← names the outside
③ CONSTRAINTS  Out of scope: say so briefly, then call escalate_to_human.          ← a ban with a destination
④ CONSTRAINTS  Fraud, chargeback or legal action: escalate at once, ask nothing.   ← trigger and action
⑤ CONSTRAINTS  Unsure: say what you couldn't determine, then escalate. No guesses. ← the long-tail fallback
⑥ OUTPUT       At most three sentences; expand only when asked.                    ← a limit code can check

The one line people skip, on one input:

🔴 Naive 🟢 Engineered
Prompt (the part that differs) Never discuss refunds over $500. Refund above $500: don't quote an amount; call escalate_to_human with the request.
On the input "refund my $800 charge" hedges, refuses vaguely, or argues itself into a partial answer one short line, then the tool call
Fails as improvised fallback; an untestable clause —
The one edit — ③ giving the prohibition a destination
Rule What actually happens
Name the outside Listing only what's in scope leaves the model to infer the boundary from silence. A named out-of-scope category gives it a line.
Narrow beats broad "Never discuss anything financial" over-triggers on invoices. A specific rule with a named exit gives a precise line.
Hedging is usually a missing path "Never state what you can't verify" with no alternative leaves qualifying everything as the only way to comply.

Evolution

Lineage:May 2024 the Model Spec publishes a behavioural spec in full2024 Anthropic publishes app system promptsJan 2026 Claude's constitution
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026): Anthropic's published app prompt has a <refusal_handling> section.
  • Stronger-model test: no. A stronger model follows a clause more closely; it can't know your scope, your escalation path or your liability. What won't change: only you can name the destination.
  • Checked on: "a destination is followed more often" is reasoned from Anthropic's guide (Oct 2026), not measured.

Measure it

  • Offline: per clause, against the prompt without it: a should-refuse cohort and a near-miss cohort in the golden set, scored for under-refusal and over-refusal.
  • In production: refusal, escalation and hedge rates per prompt version, and human overrides of refusals; a refusal rate climbing after each incident means the rules are over-tightening.
  • Enforced by: a request only, for each clause. Assertions prove it on known cases; a tool's own limits and permissions hold what must not fail.

Interview

30-second answer: A behavioural spec governs how the assistant acts: voice, scope, refusal, escalation, and when unsure. The when-unsure clause earns most, because without it the model improvises a different fallback each time. Every prohibition gets a destination, a named action, so there's one right output to test. And each rule is a classifier, so I measure over-refusal as well as under-refusal.

Q · Mechanism — Why does a refusal need a destination? A bare ban tells the model what not to produce and leaves the replacement open, so it fills that gap: a hedge, a partial answer, or an argument for an exception. A destination turns the case into a route with one correct action. That also helps you more than the model, because a specific action is what an assertion can check. Anthropic's guide (Oct 2026) gives the matching advice: say what to do, not only what to avoid.

Q · Trade-off — How do you stop the spec making the assistant useless? Measure it as a regression. The simpler rung is one narrow clause, not a broad category. Each rule has two errors, and teams only collect the first, the bad cases it should catch. I add near-miss cases that look prohibited and aren't, and gate over-refusal like under-refusal. On wording, narrow rules with a named exit over categorical bans. Without that metric, each incident makes the bot more cautious and nobody sees the product getting worse.

Pitfalls

  • "Hedging is a model trait you can prompt away with 'be confident'"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it reads like personality, so you reach for a personality fix.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: ours was our own instruction working: "never state anything you can't verify", with no alternative path, made qualifying everything the only way to comply.
    ↳ Think instead: give it somewhere to go. A when-unsure clause did what "be confident" didn't.
  • Not the same: a persona vs a spec
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both sit at the top of a system prompt and set how the assistant comes across.
    ↳ Difference: a persona sets voice. A spec sets behaviour on specific cases. Anthropic's guide wants detailed character for role-play apps; for a task bot, scope and fallback are what you can test.
    ↳ Think instead: see the role line: voice, not accuracy.
  • Don't ship a refusal rule without near-miss cases.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the incident gave you a bad case, and that's the case you test.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the rule also catches legitimate requests, nothing measures it, and the bot gets worse quietly.
    ↳ Do instead: add one near-miss with every should-refuse case. See the refusal baseline.
  • Don't write a spec for a stateless extraction call.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a template with tone and escalation blocks looks complete.
    ↳ What goes wrong: tone means nothing when the output is a JSON object, and every clause is paid per request.
    ↳ Do instead: use the simpler rung: a task and an output contract.
  • Shelf life: the wording that triggers refusals shifts with each model. Naming the destination and testing both errors won't.

Connections

Path:instruction hierarchybehavioural specstool descriptionsassertions
  • Builds on instruction writing: behaviour, threshold and fallback for one clause.
  • Used by system prompt design: these clauses fill the team layer.
  • Measured by golden datasets: the cohorts both errors are scored on.
  • Enforced by defence in depth: what holds when a clause doesn't.

notes.title: Tool Descriptions as Prompts — The Text the Model Reads at the Moment It Chooses
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: define tools · Anthropic Engineering: writing effective tools for agents · OpenAI: function calling

TL;DR

A tool's name, description and parameter docs are prompt text, read at the moment the model decides whether and how to call it. The sentence that pays most is the one people omit: when not to use this tool, and which tool to use instead, by name. The schema enforces shape. It can't express judgement, so choosing the right tool stays a request.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:a confusion pair in the logsname: verb + object + keywhat it doeswhen not, naming the other tooleach parameter's meaningwhat it doesn't returnre-run the selection eval

Recall

Prompt Answer
Most-omitted content? When not to use it, what it doesn't return, the sibling tool by name.
Anthropic's length guidance (Oct 2026)? At least 3–4 sentences per tool, more if complex.
What still holds if the model ignores this? The schema's shape and your code's permission checks, not the tool choice.

The idea

Two tools: search_accounts ("Searches accounts.") and lookup_account_by_email ("Gets an account."). A user pastes an email address and the agent calls search, gets a weak match and answers about the wrong customer. Types were correct and the call was valid; it was the wrong tool.

You didn't think of those words as a prompt, because they were generated from API code and named for developers who have the surrounding context. The model has only those words.

Rewrite them for that reader. The lookup description says what it needs and what it returns, and adds: "Do not use it to search by name or company; use search_accounts." That cross-reference addresses the exact decision the model was getting wrong, so one sentence closes a whole confusion pair.

The trade: longer descriptions cost input tokens on every request and need upkeep, and they stop helping once two tools really overlap. They're the cheap first fix to test; a real overlap needs a tool redesign.

How it works

One tool's text, read as prompt regions. What a definition contains is owned by tool schemas; this note owns the wording.

① TASK         lookup_account_by_email: retrieves a billing account from an email.  ← name carries selection
② CONSTRAINTS  Use first for any one customer's balance or invoices.                ← when to use
③ CONSTRAINTS  Not for name or company searches: use search_accounts.               ← the cross-reference
④ CONTEXT      email: the billing address, not a contact address. e.g. a@b.com      ← meaning, format, example
⑤ CONTEXT      include_invoices: default false; adds invoices to the result.        ← what a parameter costs
⑥ OUTPUT       Returns balance, plan, three recent invoices. No refund status.      ← stops invented fields

The same pair, before and after:

🔴 Naive 🟢 Engineered
Prompt (the part that differs) lookup_account_by_email: "Gets an account." regions ②, ③ and ⑥
On the input "what does a@b.com owe?" wrong tool, or the right one followed by invented fields it expected right tool; states refund status is unknown
Fails as confusion pair; fabricated fields —
The one edit — ③ naming the other tool in the description
Rule What actually happens
Name by verb, object, key lookup_account_by_email carries selection signal before a word of description. Prefix by service when tools span systems (github_list_prs).
Negative space Stating what isn't returned stops the model calling the right tool and then inventing what it expected.
Name parameters for the reader Anthropic Engineering's example: user_id, not user. Enums make an invalid value impossible, where a sentence makes it unlikely.
Ask for an explanation, not reasoning Anthropic's page (Oct 2026): a parameter asking for the model's thinking may cause a reasoning_extraction refusal.

Which tools to have is tool design; too many tools is tool selection at scale; the call itself is function calling. Providers disagree on where "when to use" goes (see the chapter map's Landscape).

Evolution

Lineage:2023 function descriptions as API docs2024 strict schemas take over shapeSep 2025 "tools are prompts" becomes written guidanceNov 2025 example calls in the definition2026 forced tool choice rejected by some Claude models, so wording steers selection
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026): Anthropic's docs call detailed descriptions "by far the most important factor" in tool performance; OpenAI gives matching advice.
  • Stronger-model test: no. A stronger model reads the text better; it can't learn what your tool doesn't return. What won't change: the model only has what you wrote.
  • Checked on: Anthropic Engineering reports refined descriptions helped Claude Sonnet 3.5 on SWE-bench Verified (2025), giving no figure.

Measure it

  • Offline: tool-selection accuracy per confusion pair on labelled tasks, against the old text; then read transcripts for invented fields.
  • In production: wrong-tool rate, argument validation failures and repeat calls, per tool and per description version.
  • Enforced by: the schema validator for shape; permission checks in the tool's code for what may run. Choosing the right tool is a request only.

Interview

30-second answer: A tool description is a prompt read at the moment of choosing. Names, parameter docs and enums all condition the model, and most teams generate them from code written for someone else. A good one says what the tool does, when not to use it and what to use instead, what each parameter means, and what it doesn't return. The schema enforces shape; selection stays a request.

Q · Mechanism — Why put this in the description, not the system prompt? Position and upkeep. The description sits beside the name and schema, so per-tool guidance is read with the decision it affects and is versioned with the tool. A rule in a shared system prompt duplicates it and drifts. OpenAI's guide does say to use the system prompt for when to use each function, so I keep cross-tool policy there and per-tool guidance here.

Q · Trade-off — Thirty tools and frequent wrong picks: more description, or fewer tools? Diagnose first, by logging chosen against expected and reading the confusion pairs. The simpler rung is wording: if errors cluster in a few pairs, add cross-references and re-test. If they're spread across many tools, text won't fix it: consolidate or defer tools, which selection at scale owns. Wording is cheap and quick to test, so it goes first.

Pitfalls

  • "Tool descriptions are API docs; terse is fine because the schema says the rest"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the code already has docstrings, and auto-generating them is free.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a schema states shape, never judgement. Which of two tools applies, or what isn't returned, can't be written in JSON Schema, and docstrings assume a reader with context.
    ↳ Think instead: write for a reader who has only these words.
  • Not the same: tool description vs tool result
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are tool text in the same conversation.
    ↳ Difference: the description is instruction you wrote. The result is data that may hold an attacker's text. A description from a third-party MCP server isn't yours either.
    ↳ Think instead: trust by who wrote it; see pinning definitions.
  • 🧙 Folklore: "CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool"
    ↳ Why it spread: it fixed undertriggering on older models, and the fix got copied.
    ↳ What the evidence says: Anthropic's guide (Oct 2026) says recent models may overtrigger on it and suggests plain "Use this tool when…".
    ↳ Do instead: write the condition plainly and measure selection on your set.
  • Don't describe your way out of a bad toolset.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: editing text is faster than changing tools.
    ↳ What goes wrong: if two tools really do overlap, no sentence separates them reliably, and every added sentence is paid per request.
    ↳ Do instead: try one cross-reference; if the pair stays confused, merge or redesign.
  • Shelf life: length guidance and overtriggering are volatile. Writing for a reader with no context is durable.

Connections

Path:tool schemastool descriptionstool designselection at scale
  • Owned elsewhere: tool-call prompting and the Agentic section own the call mechanics.
  • Used by system prompt design: per-tool rules move here.
  • Attacked by indirect prompt injection: tool results and third-party definitions.
  • Costed in context ordering: definitions sit first in the prefix.
  • Measured by component eval: selection scored on its own.
  • Drilled in tool descriptions are prompts.

notes.title: Skill and Instruction Files — Instructions That Load When They're Needed
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: Agent Skills · AGENTS.md

TL;DR

Instruction files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) load at session start and are paid every session. Skills (SKILL.md) load in stages: name and description always, the body on a match, linked files when read. So a skill's description does retrieval work: it is what the model matches against.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request

Recall

Prompt Answer
A skill's three levels? Metadata about 100 tokens; body under 5k; linked files only when read.
What triggers a skill? The model matches the request against description: what it does, when to use it.
Is any of this enforced? No. It is context; a hook or a permission blocks an action.

The idea

A long review procedure lives in the system prompt, needed rarely and paid on every request. As a skill it costs one line until it's needed. A vague description means it never fires, so the wording decides. The trade: less resident text, one more thing to test. A skill is also installed code and instructions: audit it like a dependency, and test that it triggers. Harness mechanics are owned by coding-agent harness mechanics.

Evolution

Lineage:2025 project instruction filesOct 2025 Agent SkillsDec 2025 AGENTS.md joins the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation; Agent Skills published as an open standard. 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): formats are shared, while precedence differs by tool: AGENTS.md says the closest file wins, and Claude Code concatenates every CLAUDE.md it finds.

notes.title: Meta-Prompting — A Model Writes the Prompt, and Only a Score Says It Helped
notes.html:
References

Suzgun & Kalai 2024: Meta-Prompting · OpenAI: prompt generation

TL;DR

Two senses share the name. Practical: a model writes or repairs your prompt. Paper: a coordinator model splits a task and dispatches parts to fresh expert instances of itself. Neither is optimisation until something scores the candidates.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchdesign time

Recall

Prompt Answer
The two meanings? A model writing a prompt; a coordinator dispatching to expert instances.
The line between this and APE? APE scores candidates on a set and selects; this may not.
The failure mode? A rewrite that reads better and scores worse, with nobody measuring.

The idea

You hand a model a failing prompt and ask for a better one. It returns something longer and more polished, and you ship it because it reads well. Without a set behind it you can't tell a gain from a change of style. It's good for the blank page and for variants. The trade: fast drafts in exchange for trusting nothing until the eval runs.

Evolution

Lineage:Nov 2022 APEJan 2024 Suzgun & Kalai (GPT-4)2024 vendor prompt generators and improvers. 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): the tools ship in provider consoles; OpenAI's page says DSPy-style methods may come later.

Code

A repair meta-prompt: the failures are what make it more than a restyle.

① TASK         Rewrite the prompt below so these failing cases pass.    ← a target, not "improve"
② CONSTRAINTS  Keep {{variables}}. Change as little as possible.        ← stops a full restyle
③ CONTEXT      <prompt>{{prompt}}</prompt> <failures>{{cases}}</failures> ← evidence
④ OUTPUT       The revised prompt only.                                 ← goes to the eval next

notes.title: Prompt Templating — A Value Is Data, a Template Is Code
notes.html:
References

Jinja: sandbox · Kettle 2015: server-side template injection · LangSmith: prompt template format

TL;DR

Templating turns a prompt from a string into an artifact, and it decides three things at once: who can run code, which tier a value lands in, and how many prompts you really ship. A value passed into a template is data. Text that becomes the template is code. Almost every hazard is one crossing that line. Compose fixed fragments above the cache line; keep conditionals below it.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:template + valuessandboxrenderoutside values into the user turn onlystrip and wrapcanonical bytesthe rendered text loggedmodel

Recall

Prompt Answer
When do braces in user text crash format? Only when the text becomes part of the template, not a value.
Why does a tenant template need a sandbox? Template text reaches Python objects; unsandboxed Jinja is code execution.
How many prompts do N flags make? 2^N renderings; six independent flags make 64.

The idea

A team lets tenants edit their prompt template. One tenant saves {{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() }}. That isn't prompt injection: it runs in your server, before any model sees anything. Meanwhile a second feature builds its template by pasting the customer's message into the string and then calling .format(), and any JSON in a message raises KeyError.

Both bugs are the same one. Text you didn't write crossed from value to template. A value is inserted once and never parsed again, so braces in it are harmless. Template text is parsed by the engine. Keep outside text on the value side, and render tenant-written templates in a sandbox.

A third hazard is silent. Conditionals turn one template into many prompts, and each branch above the cache line is another prefix.

Your code enforces all of this. What it can't do is make a value harmless to the model.

The trade: a stricter renderer and fewer conditionals cost authoring convenience, and buy prompts you can enumerate, test and cache.

How it works

The render path. Two questions decide who can run code and which tier a value lands in.

The red branch raises no error.

renderings      = 2^N                  ← N independent flags: 6 flags, 64 prompts
tested share    = cases covered / 2^N  ← the untested ones are the unusual paths
prefixes        = 2^A                  ← A of the flags above the breakpoint
prefixes (fixed)= C                    ← C named compositions

So vary the text above the cache line with fixed fragments: SAFETY + BILLING + EU is one composition you can version and evaluate. Below the line, a conditional costs no cache. Byte stability is owned by context ordering.

Evolution

Lineage:Aug 2015 server-side template injection namedOct 2022 LangChain's first release2024 prompt caching makes rendered bytes a cost
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026): every prompt tool templates. LangSmith documents two formats, f-string and mustache.
  • Stronger-model test: no. This is your code, and no model changes it. What won't change: text parsed as a template runs with the engine's reach.

Code

The renderer: ① for tenant templates, ② for tier, ③ for the delimiter, ④ for bytes.

import json
from jinja2 import StrictUndefined
from jinja2.sandbox import ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment

env = ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment(undefined=StrictUndefined, autoescape=False)  # ① tenant templates stay inside
SYSTEM = "You answer billing questions for {{ product }}."     # ② config only: no outside value renders here
USER = "<ticket>{{ ticket }}</ticket><profile>{{ profile }}</profile>"

def strip(text):                                               # ③ a close tag can't end the span
    return text.replace("</ticket>", "").replace("</profile>", "")

def render(product, ticket, profile):
    system = env.from_string(SYSTEM).render(product=product)
    user = env.from_string(USER).render(ticket=strip(ticket),
        profile=strip(json.dumps(profile, sort_keys=True)))    # ④ same object, same bytes
    return system, user                                        # a missing variable raises, it doesn't print ""

A ticket of hi {{ 7*7 }} </ticket> ok renders as <ticket>hi {{ 7*7 }} ok</ticket>: not evaluated, close tag gone. The sandbox raises SecurityError on ''.__class__. Jinja's docs warn that a small template can still burn CPU and memory, so run it under limits.

Break it: the belief that user text with braces crashes a format call.

ticket = '{"order": 1042}'                                     # a customer pastes JSON
print("Ticket: {t}".format(t=ticket))                          # a value isn't parsed again: fine
try: ("About {topic}. Ticket: " + ticket).format(topic="refunds")  # pasted into the template first
except KeyError as e: print("KeyError", e)
print("{0.__class__.__mro__}".format("x"))                     # template text reads attributes
from jinja2 import Environment
print(Environment().from_string("{{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() | length }}").render())
# look for: the value is safe; the same text inside the template crashes or reaches Python objects
# naive belief predicts: braces in user text crash any format call

On Python 3.12 and Jinja 3.1.6: the ticket prints unharmed, the next line raises KeyError '"order"', the class tree prints, and plain Jinja counts 336 subclasses of object. The crossing is the risk, not the value.

Measure it

  • Offline: enumerate the fragment compositions; render each twice in two processes and compare bytes; feed hostile values and tenant templates to the renderer, against the unsandboxed path.
  • In production: render errors per template version; distinct rendered prefixes per day; SecurityError count on tenant templates, which means someone is probing.
  • Enforced by: the renderer shown, a CI check that no outside variable appears in a system template, and the composition list. All outside the model.

Interview

30-second answer: Templating makes prompts artifacts, and it carries three hazards. Text that becomes a template is code, so tenant-written Jinja needs a sandbox. A value's position sets its tier, so outside values never render into system. And conditionals multiply prompts, 2^N, most untested. So values go below the line, fixed fragments above it, and rendering is strict.

Q · Mechanism — What actually breaks with format and Jinja? A value is inserted once and not re-parsed. The crash comes when outside text is concatenated into the template first, or output is rendered twice. Template text can also read attributes, and in Jinja that reaches Python, so an untrusted template is code execution. A sandbox intercepts attribute access.

Q · Trade-off — Conditionals, or several flat prompts? The simpler rung is one flat prompt per endpoint, and I'd stay there while there are a few. Duplication then drifts: eight copies of a safety clause, one missed in a policy change. Composition fixes that without conditionals: fixed fragments in a fixed order, varied by which ones are included. Each composition is one versioned artifact, so the cache sees few prefixes. Conditionals are fine below the cache line, where the text varies anyway.

Pitfalls

  • "User braces will crash our f-string"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: format strings use braces, so user braces look like syntax, and a crash in this area is easy to remember.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a value isn't parsed. It crashes only when outside text becomes template text, as Break it shows.
    ↳ Think instead: ask which side of the line the text is on. Then fix the crossing, not the character.
  • "Escaping the input makes interpolation safe"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: escaping is the fix for SQL and for HTML.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: escaping fixes parsing, not trust. Perfectly escaped text in the system message still sits in the system message, and the model still reads it.
    ↳ Think instead: placement decides the tier; escaping only protects the template.
  • Not the same: template injection vs prompt injection
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are untrusted text getting interpreted, and both say "injection".
    ↳ Difference: template injection runs on your server, before the model, and a sandbox can stop it. Prompt injection is read by the model, and nothing fully stops it.
    ↳ Think instead: the first is an engine bug, the second a channel problem.
  • Don't build a template language for three prompts.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: partials, inheritance and flags feel like clean engineering.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the shipped prompt can no longer be read without running the engine, and evals cover a few of its forms.
    ↳ Do instead: flat files first; fixed fragments when a clause needs one source of truth.
  • Shelf life: tool names and formats change. The line between a value and a template doesn't.

Connections

Path:system prompt designprompt templatingcontext orderingprompt versioning
  • Builds on system, user and prefill: no outside variable in system.
  • Attacked by prompt injection: the value the renderer can't make safe.
  • Used by the prompt-layer architecture: one place that renders.
  • Measured by regression suites: a suite per composition.
  • Drilled in design the prompt layer.

notes.title: Multi-Agent Prompt Design — The Brief Is the Whole Interface
notes.html:
References

Anthropic Engineering: multi-agent research system

TL;DR

A sub-agent sees only what it was told, so the prompting job moves from one big instruction to briefs: objective, output format, tools and sources, boundary. This note is a pointer: the delegation contract owns what crosses the boundary, and orchestrator-worker owns the orchestration.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why must a brief be self-contained? Separate context windows: nothing is shared implicitly.
The four parts of a brief? Objective, output format, tools and sources, task boundary.
The classic failure? Vague briefs: workers misread the task or duplicate each other.

The idea

Anthropic's early lead agent wrote briefs like "research the semiconductor shortage". One worker studied the 2021 automotive crisis, and two duplicated each other on 2025 supply chains. Each brief is a prompt, and the fix is prompt text. The trade: a longer brief per delegation, for workers that don't overlap. Roles earn their place through tools and permissions, not titles.

Evolution

Lineage: Jun 2025 Anthropic's four-part brief. 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): its guide now warns that recent models over-delegate, so say when not to use sub-agents.

Code

① TASK         Find 2025 chip supply-chain changes for carmakers.    ← one objective
② CONTEXT      Decided: 2025 only; the lead covers 2021.             ← what won't transfer otherwise
③ CONSTRAINTS  Use filings and search. Don't cover pricing.          ← tools and boundary
④ OUTPUT       {"findings": [...], "sources": [...]}, 200 words max. ← what comes back
